question: The Iliad opens with one word in Greek: menis — wrath. Agamemnon, king of Mycenae and commander of the Greek army at Troy, had been forced to give up his war-prize, the captive princess Chryseis, after Apollo sent a plague through the Greek camp. To restore his honor in front of his army, Agamemnon seized the captive Briseis from Achilles's tent instead. Achilles, son of the sea-nymph Thetis and the mightiest warrior of the Greeks, drew his sword to kill Agamemnon on the spot — but the goddess Athena appeared, visible only to him, and grabbed him by his golden hair. She told him to put the sword away and use words instead. What did Achilles do as a result of the quarrel?
answer: Withdrew from the war and sulked in his tent, asking Zeus to let the Greeks lose
choices: Withdrew from the war and sulked in his tent, asking Zeus to let the Greeks lose
Killed Agamemnon in single combat the following morning at sunrise
Sailed home to Phthia with his Myrmidon warriors and abandoned the cause
Took command of the Greek army by forcing Agamemnon to abdicate
context: Achilles's mother Thetis went to Olympus and persuaded Zeus to honor her son by letting the Trojans push the Greeks back to their ships. The result was disaster after disaster for the Greeks — the entire Iliad turns on this one moment of stolen honor.

question: After weeks of Greek defeats with Achilles sulking in his tent, Agamemnon sent an embassy of three men to beg him to return to the battle. He offered enormous reparations: seven tripods, ten talents of gold, twenty cauldrons, twelve racehorses, seven captive women including Briseis untouched, and his own daughter in marriage with seven cities as dowry. The three ambassadors were Odysseus (master of words), Ajax (mighty in arms), and an old man who had been Achilles's tutor since boyhood. The old man told Achilles the long story of his own life, weeping, begging Achilles not to let his hard heart destroy him. Achilles still refused. Who was the old tutor whose plea Achilles rejected?
answer: Phoenix
choices: Phoenix
Nestor
Chiron
Peleus
context: Phoenix had raised Achilles like a son, cutting his meat and holding the cup to his lips as a child. His tearful argument was that even prayers and the Litai (the limping daughters of Zeus) can soften a great man's wrath. Achilles softened slightly — telling Phoenix to stay the night and decide in the morning whether to go home with him.

question: With Achilles still refusing to fight and the Greeks being slaughtered at their own ships, his closest companion Patroclus came to him weeping. Trojan fire was already burning the lead ship. Patroclus begged for permission to wear Achilles's own armor and lead the Myrmidons into battle himself — just to scare the Trojans into retreat. Achilles agreed but warned him: drive the Trojans away from the ships, then come back. Do not pursue them to the walls of Troy. Patroclus put on the famous armor and led the charge. The Trojans, thinking Achilles himself had returned, fled in panic. Patroclus pursued them all the way to Troy's gates. Who killed Patroclus there?
answer: Hector, with help from Apollo who stunned Patroclus first
choices: Hector, with help from Apollo who stunned Patroclus first
Paris, with a single arrow through the heel
Aeneas, in single combat by the Scaean Gate
Sarpedon, son of Zeus, before falling himself
context: Apollo struck Patroclus from behind, knocking the helmet from his head and the spear from his hand. A Trojan named Euphorbus wounded him next. Hector finished him with a spear through the belly. Patroclus's dying words promised Hector that Achilles would kill him in turn — within days.

question: After Achilles killed Hector in revenge for Patroclus's death, he dragged Hector's corpse three times around the walls of Troy behind his chariot, then back to his camp where he refused to give it up for burial. For twelve days the body lay in the dust outside Achilles's tent while Achilles wept by Patroclus's pyre. On the twelfth night, an old man slipped through the Greek camp guided by Hermes in disguise. The old man was King Priam of Troy, Hector's father, who had fifty sons and had now lost the greatest of them. He walked alone into Achilles's tent and knelt at his feet. What did Priam do that made Achilles weep with him through the night?
answer: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
choices: Kissed the hands that had killed his son
Laid a king's crown of gold at Achilles's feet
Begged Achilles to take him as a slave in Hector's place
Pressed a dagger into Achilles's palm and asked to die
context: The scene is the moral climax of the Iliad: Priam, the old enemy king, kissing the hands of his son's killer. Achilles thought of his own father Peleus, who would also lose a beloved son soon, and they wept together. Achilles ransomed Hector's body and granted Troy twelve days of truce for the funeral.

question: After Achilles finally allowed Patroclus's body to be burned on a great pyre — with twelve captive Trojan youths sacrificed beside him, four horses, two dogs, and jars of honey and oil — he held the most lavish funeral games ever described in Greek epic. There were chariot races, boxing matches, wrestling, foot races, armed combat with sharp spears, archery contests at a tethered dove, a shot-put with a lump of iron, and a contest in spear-throwing. Achilles judged each event personally and awarded magnificent prizes from his own wealth. In the chariot race, the wisest competitor was an old man giving advice to his son. Who was the old man advising his son Antilochus during the chariot race?
answer: Nestor, king of Pylos
choices: Nestor, king of Pylos
Odysseus, king of Ithaca
Idomeneus, king of Crete
Diomedes, king of Argos
context: Nestor told Antilochus that brains beat horsepower — to hug the turning post tightly, take the curve as sharp as possible without crashing. Antilochus took second place against faster teams by following the advice. The chariot race in Iliad Book 23 is one of the most detailed sports scenes in all of ancient literature.

question: After ten years of failed siege at Troy, the Greek army built a hollow wooden horse so large it had to be left on the beach. The Greeks burned their camp, boarded their ships, and sailed out of sight behind the island of Tenedos. They left behind only one man, captured by the Trojans, who told a long convincing lie. He said his name was Sinon and that the Greeks had voted to sacrifice him to Athena before sailing home, but he escaped. The horse, he said, was an offering to Athena to atone for stealing the Palladium — too large to fit through Troy's gates, so the Trojans would either leave it or break their own walls to drag it in. He claimed bringing it inside would guarantee Troy's survival. What was the horse actually filled with?
answer: About thirty Greek warriors led by Odysseus and Menelaus, hidden inside
choices: About thirty Greek warriors led by Odysseus and Menelaus, hidden inside
Casks of Greek wine drugged to poison the Trojan defenders
Bronze weapons for a Greek traitor inside Troy to distribute
Statues of the Greek gods carved by Athena's own priests
context: The story is told in Virgil's Aeneid Book 2 by Aeneas to Queen Dido. The men inside breathed through carved nostrils. That night Sinon opened a hatch in the horse's belly and signaled the fleet to return. The hidden warriors climbed down ropes, opened the gates from inside, and Troy fell before dawn.

question: When the Greeks left their huge wooden horse on the beach outside Troy, most of the Trojans wanted to drag it inside as a war-trophy. One Trojan priest of Poseidon refused. He hurled his spear into the horse's flank — the spear stuck, quivering, and from inside came a hollow metallic clang from the armor of the hidden Greeks. He shouted at his countrymen the warning that became proverbial in Latin: Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes — I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts. As he stood there shouting, two enormous sea serpents rose from the waves near the island of Tenedos and swam straight for the shore. They wrapped themselves around the priest and his two young sons and crushed all three to death in front of the watching Trojans. What was the name of the priest the serpents killed?
answer: Laocoon
choices: Laocoon
Helenus
Chryses
Calchas
context: The Trojans took the killing as proof Laocoon had blasphemed the goddess Athena's offering — and dragged the horse inside. The death of Laocoon is the subject of a famous Hellenistic marble statue rediscovered in Rome in 1506, which Michelangelo studied and which deeply influenced Renaissance sculpture.

question: After Achilles killed Hector, the war dragged on. Achilles fought brilliantly until one day at the Scaean Gate of Troy, the cowardly Trojan prince Paris — the one who had started the whole war by stealing Helen — drew his bow from the shelter of the wall. Apollo guided the arrow. It struck Achilles in the one place on his body where he could be wounded. As an infant his mother Thetis had dipped him in the river Styx to make him immortal, holding him by one part that the dark water never touched. That part was the only mortal spot on his body. Where did the arrow strike Achilles?
answer: His heel, where his mother had held him as a baby
choices: His heel, where his mother had held him as a baby
The hollow of his throat, where her thumb had pressed
The small of his back, where her palm had cradled him
Behind his left ear, where her fingers had rested
context: The phrase 'Achilles heel' for a hero's one weak point comes from this story. After his death, Achilles's armor — forged by the smith god Hephaestus — was awarded to Odysseus rather than Ajax, who went mad with rage and killed himself by falling on his own sword.

question: Cassandra was a princess of Troy, daughter of King Priam and Queen Hecuba and twin sister of the prophet Helenus. The god Apollo fell in love with her and offered her the gift of perfect prophecy if she would lie with him. She agreed, accepted the gift, and then refused him. Apollo could not take the gift back — but he could twist it. He spat into her mouth. Cassandra would see the future clearly forever — every disaster, every betrayal, every death. She warned the Trojans that the wooden horse was a trap. She warned that Paris bringing Helen to Troy would destroy the city. She warned her brother Hector not to fight Achilles. What was the curse Apollo added to her gift?
answer: No one would ever believe her prophecies
choices: No one would ever believe her prophecies
She would lose the power of human speech entirely
Every prophecy would come true the opposite way
She would forget each prophecy moments after speaking it
context: Cassandra was taken as a war-prize by Agamemnon after Troy fell. She predicted she and Agamemnon would both be murdered by his wife Clytemnestra when they reached Mycenae — no one believed her. They were murdered exactly as she had said, axed in the bath, on the day they arrived.

question: The Trojan War began at a wedding — the marriage of the sea-nymph Thetis (who would later become Achilles's mother) to the mortal king Peleus. Every god and goddess was invited except Eris, the goddess of strife. Furious at the snub, Eris hurled a golden apple into the wedding hall inscribed with two words: To the Fairest. Three goddesses each claimed it: Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite. Zeus refused to judge between his wife, his daughter, and the goddess of love. He sent Hermes to find the most handsome mortal man in the world to decide the case. The chosen mortal was a young Trojan prince tending sheep on Mount Ida, who did not know he was royal. The three goddesses each offered him a bribe. What did Aphrodite offer Paris that won her the apple?
answer: The most beautiful woman in the world as his wife, Helen of Sparta
choices: The most beautiful woman in the world as his wife, Helen of Sparta
Wisdom enough to rule both Greece and Troy together
An empire stretching from Egypt to the Black Sea
Immortality and a seat on Olympus beside the gods
context: Helen was already married to King Menelaus of Sparta when Paris sailed to claim his prize. Paris carried her back to Troy. Menelaus called on the oath every Greek suitor of Helen had sworn — to defend whoever won her hand. A thousand ships sailed for Troy. The war lasted ten years and ended in the city's destruction.

question: On his long voyage home from Troy, Odysseus and twelve of his men landed on an island of one-eyed giants called Cyclopes. They entered a huge cave full of cheese and lambs and waited for the owner to return. The owner was a Cyclops named Polyphemus, son of the sea god Poseidon. He rolled a stone across the cave mouth so heavy that twenty wagons could not move it, sealing the Greeks inside. Then he picked up two of Odysseus's men, dashed their brains out against the floor like puppies, and ate them raw for dinner. For breakfast he ate two more, for the next dinner two more. Odysseus could not kill him in his sleep — they would all be trapped behind the stone. What clever name did Odysseus give Polyphemus when the giant asked it?
answer: Nobody
choices: Nobody
Mighty One
Greekfriend
Stranger
context: Odysseus got the giant drunk on strong wine, then drove a sharpened wooden stake through his single eye. Polyphemus roared for help. The other Cyclopes came running and asked who was hurting him. He shouted 'Nobody is killing me!' — and they left, thinking he was sick or mad. Odysseus and his surviving men escaped tied beneath the bellies of the giant's rams.

question: After blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus and escaping his cave by clinging beneath the bellies of his rams, Odysseus and his surviving men ran for their ship and rowed for their lives. Once safely at sea, Odysseus could not resist taunting the giant on the shore — even though his crew begged him not to. He shouted his real name across the water, telling Polyphemus exactly who had blinded him and where he was from, so the giant could curse him properly. Polyphemus then prayed to his father Poseidon for revenge. What specifically did Polyphemus pray for that Poseidon granted?
answer: That Odysseus never reach home, or if he did, that he arrive alone on a stranger's ship
choices: That Odysseus never reach home, or if he did, that he arrive alone on a stranger's ship
That Odysseus drown in the wine-dark sea before sunset of that same day
That Odysseus's entire bloodline be wiped utterly from the face of the earth
That Odysseus be blinded in turn by the hand of his own son at Ithaca
context: Poseidon granted every word. Odysseus lost all twelve ships and every one of his men. He arrived home alone, on a Phaeacian ship that put him ashore asleep, to find his palace overrun by suitors devouring his wealth. The taunt — letting pride overcome wisdom — cost Odysseus ten extra years of wandering.

question: The witch Circe told Odysseus he could not sail home until he had crossed Ocean to the edge of the world and consulted a single dead prophet in the underworld. Odysseus sailed to a dim shore where two rivers met, dug a pit with his sword, and poured offerings of milk, honey, wine, water, and barley into it. He then cut the throats of a black ram and a black ewe over the pit. The ghosts of the dead came swarming up from below to drink the blood — but Odysseus held them off with his sword until the one ghost he needed had drunk and could speak truth. Which blind prophet did Odysseus need to consult?
answer: Tiresias of Thebes
choices: Tiresias of Thebes
Calchas the seer of Mycenae
Helenus the Trojan prophet
Chiron the centaur of Pelion
context: Tiresias told Odysseus exactly what would happen and how to survive it: avoid eating the cattle of the sun god Helios on the island of Thrinacia, find his palace overrun by suitors, kill them, and then go on a final pilgrimage inland carrying an oar until he met someone who mistook it for a winnowing fan. Tiresias had been blinded by Hera and given prophecy by Zeus.

question: Among the ghosts Odysseus saw in the underworld was his old comrade Achilles — the mightiest warrior of the Greeks, now a pale shade among the dead. Odysseus tried to comfort him: in life Achilles had been worshipped like a god, in death he ruled over all the other souls in the underworld, so surely he had no cause to grieve. Achilles cut him off with one of the most-quoted lines in Greek literature. What did Achilles say he would rather be?
answer: A poor hired laborer on a poor man's farm in the sunlight than king of all the dead
choices: A poor hired laborer on a poor man's farm in the sunlight than king of all the dead
A wounded slave in a Persian copper mine than commander of an army
A blind beggar at the gates of Troy than a prince in shining armor
A nameless oarsman on a merchant ship than a hero in songs
context: The line is in Odyssey Book 11. Achilles asked desperately after his son Neoptolemus and his old father Peleus, then drifted away across the field of asphodel. The line reverses the heroic ideal of the Iliad — death and glory are no longer the highest good. Life itself, however humble, is.

question: In the underworld, Odysseus saw the ghost of his own mother Anticleia approaching the blood pit. He had left her alive at Ithaca when he sailed for Troy twenty years before. He did not know she had died. After he let her drink and she spoke, she explained she had not died of sickness or violence, but of something else. She had wasted away day after day for one specific reason. Odysseus tried three times to embrace her and three times her ghost slipped through his arms like smoke. What had killed Anticleia?
answer: Grief and longing for her absent son
choices: Grief and longing for her absent son
Plague brought by a Phoenician trader to Ithaca
A fall from the high cliff above the harbor at dawn
Poison given by one of Penelope's bolder suitors
context: Anticleia told Odysseus that Penelope was still faithful, that his old father Laertes had retired to the country, and that his young son Telemachus was nearly grown. She comforted him with the news. The scene of Odysseus trying to hug his mother's ghost three times became a template — Virgil repeated it almost word for word when Aeneas met his father Anchises in the underworld.

question: Odysseus returned home to Ithaca after twenty years to find his palace overrun by 108 suitors competing to marry his wife Penelope, eating his livestock and drinking his wine. Disguised by Athena as a filthy old beggar, he entered his own great hall unrecognized. Penelope announced a contest: she would marry whichever suitor could string her husband's old hunting bow and shoot a single arrow straight through the round holes in the heads of twelve axe-heads lined up in a row. Suitor after suitor struggled — they could not even bend the bow enough to slip the string onto its end. The old beggar then asked if he could try. The suitors laughed and Penelope agreed. What did Odysseus do after stringing the bow and putting the first arrow through all twelve axe-heads?
answer: Turned the bow on the suitors and shot them down one by one
choices: Turned the bow on the suitors and shot them down one by one
Revealed his identity and demanded their formal surrender
Sent his son Telemachus to summon the Ithacan elders to judge them
Smashed the bow over his knee to deny it to anyone else
context: Odysseus shot the ringleader Antinous through the throat with the first shot, as Antinous lifted a wine cup to his lips. Then Telemachus, the loyal swineherd Eumaeus, and the cowherd Philoetius joined him with spears. Athena added confusion to the suitors' minds. All 108 were killed. Twelve disloyal maidservants were hanged afterward in a row.

question: After Odysseus killed the 108 suitors in his great hall, Penelope still would not believe it was really her husband returned. He had been gone twenty years; gods and impostors might trick a woman. She tested him in front of the household. She ordered her maidservant Eurycleia to move their marriage bed out of their bedroom and make it up for the stranger in the hall. Odysseus flew into a rage. Their bed could NOT be moved, he shouted — because of one specific structural feature he had built into it as a young man. What was it?
answer: One bedpost was a living olive tree, rooted in the floor with the bedroom built around it
choices: One bedpost was a living olive tree, rooted in the floor with the bedroom built around it
Its four legs were sunk into the bedrock beneath the palace foundation stones
It was carved from a single block of fragrant cedar that weighed almost two tons
Bronze pegs the size of fighting spears nailed the great frame to the marble floor
context: Only Odysseus and Penelope herself knew that secret. Hearing him describe the olive tree, Penelope collapsed weeping into his arms. They spent that night in the unmoved bed — and Athena held back the dawn so the night could last longer than any other in mortal memory.

question: The witch Circe warned Odysseus he would have to sail past the island of the Sirens — winged women who sang so beautifully that every sailor who heard them steered his ship onto their rocks and died. Their meadow was white with the bones of men. Circe told him exactly how to survive both hearing the song and surviving the rocks. Odysseus melted down a large wheel of beeswax with his sword and warmed it in the sun. He then plugged the ears of every man at the oars. What did he order his men to do to him, so that he alone could hear the song?
answer: Lash him upright to the mast and refuse to free him no matter how hard he begged
choices: Lash him upright to the mast and refuse to free him no matter how hard he begged
Force him to chain himself in the cargo hold below decks for the day
Cover his eyes with a strip of leather to remove the temptation to look
Drug him unconscious with strong wine until the danger was past
context: Odysseus heard the Sirens promise to sing him everything that had happened at Troy and everything that happens on the wide earth. He thrashed and begged to be freed; his men, ears plugged, only rowed harder and tightened the ropes. Once past the island the Sirens, defeated, are said to have thrown themselves into the sea. Odysseus is the only man in Greek myth to hear them and live.

question: Past the Sirens, Odysseus had to navigate a narrow strait between two monsters. On one side was a monster called Charybdis, who three times a day swallowed the entire sea down a whirlpool large enough to drink a ship whole, then vomited it back up — any ship within reach was utterly destroyed. On the other side, a cave high in a cliff held the six-headed monster Scylla, who shot her six long necks out and snatched six sailors from any ship passing too close, holding them in the air to scream while she devoured them at leisure. Circe had told Odysseus he could not avoid both. What did Odysseus choose?
answer: Steer closer to Scylla and lose six men rather than lose every man to Charybdis
choices: Steer closer to Scylla and lose six men rather than lose every man to Charybdis
Risk the whirlpool of Charybdis to leave all his men intact aboard ship
Sail at midnight when both monsters were said to sleep below the waves
Sacrifice a black ram to Poseidon to calm the strait completely
context: Six men were snatched from the deck. Odysseus described them screaming above him as the worst thing he saw in all his wanderings. The expression 'between Scylla and Charybdis' for an impossible choice between two evils comes from this passage of Odyssey Book 12.

question: On his long voyage home, Odysseus landed at the island of Aeaea, ruled by a witch-goddess who lived in a marble palace surrounded by tame lions and wolves — once men, transformed. Half of Odysseus's crew, sent inland to explore, accepted her hospitality and ate her enchanted feast. Wagging tails like dogs around her chair, they were tapped with her wand and transformed into pigs, then driven squealing into a sty. One terrified man, Eurylochus, ran back to the ship to tell Odysseus. Odysseus marched to the palace alone — and Hermes met him on the path with a magical herb that would protect him from her spell. What was the herb the god Hermes gave him?
answer: Moly — a black-rooted plant with a milk-white flower
choices: Moly — a black-rooted plant with a milk-white flower
Nepenthe — a silver leaf that erased pain and memory
Asphodel — the pale lily of the underworld meadows
Lotus — the golden fruit that destroyed all desire for home
context: Hermes told Odysseus to drink Circe's cup unafraid, then draw his sword the instant she tapped him with her wand. Circe, astonished he was immune, dropped her wand and offered her bed. Odysseus first made her swear an oath to harm none of his men. She kept the oath — restored his men from pigs to bigger and handsomer men than before, and the crew spent a happy year on her island before sailing on.

question: Hercules was the son of Zeus by a mortal woman named Alcmene, born to be the greatest of all Greek heroes. Hera, the wife of Zeus, hated him from his birth and tried to kill him in his cradle with two huge snakes — the infant Hercules strangled them in his fists. He grew up, married Princess Megara of Thebes, and they had three sons together. Then Hera struck him with a fit of madness. In the madness, he thought his own wife and children were enemies attacking his home. He killed all of them with his own hands — Megara and the three small boys. When his sanity returned and he saw what he had done, he wanted to kill himself. The oracle at Delphi told him what penance he had to perform to atone. What was the penance?
answer: Serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform any twelve labors the king commanded
choices: Serve King Eurystheus for twelve years and perform any twelve labors the king commanded
Build a temple to Hera with his own hands stone by stone for ten years
Wander the world as a beggar for life, never speaking his real name
Carry the heads of his dead sons in a sack until they crumbled to dust
context: Eurystheus was a cousin of Hercules and a coward who hated him. He chose the twelve labors specifically to kill Hercules — each task was meant to be impossible. The completion of the labors made Hercules immortal. Euripides wrote the great tragedy of the madness; Seneca later rewrote it for Roman audiences.

question: Hercules's second labor was to kill the Lernaean Hydra, a many-headed water serpent living in the swamps near Lerna. Her breath was poison; her blood was poison; she had nine heads and the middle one was immortal. When Hercules cut off one head with his sword, two more grew back from the stump. He could not keep up with the multiplication. He called his nephew Iolaus to help. Hercules cut off each head while Iolaus did something specific to each stump immediately after — and this stopped the regrowth. What did Iolaus do?
answer: Cauterized the bleeding stump with a flaming torch
choices: Cauterized the bleeding stump with a flaming torch
Sealed the wound with wet river clay packed thick
Wrapped the stump in lion-skin to smother the regrowth
Poured sea water over the cut to drown the new heads
context: Hercules buried the immortal middle head under a huge rock by the road. King Eurystheus refused to count this labor because Hercules had used help. Hercules dipped his arrows in the Hydra's poisoned blood — those arrows would later kill the centaur Nessus, and indirectly cause Hercules's own death decades later.

question: Hercules's eleventh labor was to fetch the golden apples of the Hesperides, the nymphs who guarded a tree given to Hera by Gaia as a wedding present. The tree grew at the western edge of the world and was watched by a hundred-headed dragon called Ladon. The Hesperides were daughters of the Titan Atlas, who stood at the western edge of the world holding up the sky on his shoulders forever as punishment for the Titan war. Hercules offered Atlas a deal: he would hold up the sky for a few hours if Atlas would fetch the apples from his own daughters. Atlas agreed and brought back three apples — then offered to deliver them to Eurystheus himself, leaving Hercules holding the sky forever. How did Hercules trick Atlas back?
answer: Asked Atlas to hold the sky for one moment while he padded his shoulders with his cloak
choices: Asked Atlas to hold the sky for one moment while he padded his shoulders with his cloak
Showed Atlas a vision of his daughters being captured by pirates
Threw the golden apples at Atlas's feet so he would drop the sky to grab them
Promised Atlas he would free him forever once the apples reached Greece
context: Atlas, eager to start his trip, set down the apples and took the sky back so Hercules could pad his shoulders. Hercules picked up the apples and walked away. Athena later returned the apples to the Hesperides — they belonged to the gods, not to a mortal king. The fooling of Atlas became proverbial in Greek for outsmarting brute force.

question: Hercules's twelfth and final labor was the most terrifying: to descend alive to the underworld and bring back Cerberus, the three-headed dog who guarded the gates of Hades against any soul who tried to leave. King Eurystheus added the condition that Hercules must use no weapon. Hercules first sought initiation in the Eleusinian Mysteries to prepare his soul for the journey to the land of the dead, then descended through a cave at Cape Tainaron in the Peloponnese with the gods Hermes and Athena guiding him. He approached the throne of Hades himself and asked permission, politely. Hades agreed on one specific condition. What did Hades demand of Hercules?
answer: Subdue Cerberus bare-handed without a single weapon
choices: Subdue Cerberus bare-handed without a single weapon
Bring the dog back within three days of taking him
Leave one of his own children behind as hostage in Hades
Sacrifice a hundred black bulls at the river Styx beforehand
context: Hercules wrestled all three of Cerberus's heads at once until the great dog submitted. He carried the beast up alive to the surface and presented him at the court of Eurystheus, who took one look and dove into a large bronze jar in terror, ordering Hercules to take the dog away. Hercules returned Cerberus peacefully to the gates of Hades.

question: Hercules's fifth labor was to clean the stables of King Augeas of Elis in a single day. Augeas owned more cattle than any king in Greece — three thousand head of cattle, immortal and divine, whose dung had not been removed from their stables for thirty years. The stench killed crops for miles around. Eurystheus chose this labor specifically to humiliate Hercules: the mightiest hero of the world reduced to a manure-shoveler with no chance of finishing in a single day. What did Hercules do to clean the stables?
answer: Diverted two rivers, the Alpheus and Peneus, to flow through the stables and wash them clean
choices: Diverted two rivers, the Alpheus and Peneus, to flow through the stables and wash them clean
Carved a chariot-wide drain through bedrock with his bare hands in one morning
Set the entire mountain of dung on fire with one of his Hydra-poisoned arrows
Yoked the three thousand cattle to drag the dung-pile into the sea at once
context: Augeas had promised Hercules a tenth of the cattle as payment but then refused, claiming Hercules had only obeyed Eurystheus. Eurystheus also refused to count the labor because Hercules had been paid (or tried to be). Hercules later returned with an army, killed Augeas, and gave the kingdom to Augeas's son who had testified honestly about the promised payment.

question: Years after completing his twelve labors, Hercules took a new wife named Deianira. As they traveled together, they came to a river where the centaur Nessus offered to carry Deianira across on his back while Hercules swam. Halfway across, Nessus tried to assault her. Hercules shot the centaur from the far bank with one of his arrows poisoned in the Hydra's blood. As Nessus lay dying, he told Deianira a final lie: take some of his blood and save it; if Hercules ever stopped loving her, smear a robe with the blood and have him wear it, and his love would return. Years later Deianira heard Hercules had taken a captive princess as concubine. What happened when Hercules put on the robe Deianira sent him?
answer: The Hydra poison in Nessus's blood burned into his flesh and could not be removed
choices: The Hydra poison in Nessus's blood burned into his flesh and could not be removed
He fell instantly in love again with Deianira as Nessus had promised
He turned to stone where he stood and never moved again
His memory was wiped clean of the last twenty years of his life
context: Hercules tried to tear the robe off and it ripped his flesh with it. In agony beyond bearing, he built his own funeral pyre on Mount Oeta. Deianira hanged herself from grief when she learned what Nessus's blood actually was. Sophocles wrote the great tragedy Trachiniae about this moment.

question: Burning alive in the poisoned shirt of Nessus, Hercules climbed to the top of Mount Oeta in Thessaly. There he built an enormous pyre of oak logs with his own hands, climbed onto it, and lay down on his lion-skin cloak with his great club beside him. He asked the men with him to light it. They refused — to burn the greatest hero of Greece alive seemed like murder. He offered his bow and arrows as a gift to whichever man would light it. One young man finally agreed, took the bow, and lit the wood. As the flames roared up, a thunderclap split the sky and Zeus's chariot descended through the smoke. Who was the young man who lit the pyre and took the bow?
answer: Philoctetes
choices: Philoctetes
Iolaus
Telamon
Hylas
context: Zeus carried Hercules's mortal portion up into the smoke where it was burned away. His divine portion rose to Mount Olympus where he was made a full god, reconciled to Hera, and married her daughter Hebe the cupbearer. Philoctetes inherited the bow with the Hydra-poisoned arrows and used it ten years later to kill Paris and end the Trojan War.

question: Hercules's third labor was to capture the Ceryneian Hind, a deer with golden antlers and bronze hooves who was sacred to the goddess Artemis. The hind could outrun an arrow. Hercules pursued her for an entire year across mountains and through forests, never letting her stop to rest until at last she stopped to drink at a stream and he caught her. As he carried her back, Artemis herself appeared on the path with her brother Apollo, furious that her sacred animal had been touched. Hercules had to convince her not to kill him on the spot. What did Hercules say that saved his life?
answer: He had been ordered by Eurystheus, who would bear the blame and return the hind unharmed
choices: He had been ordered by Eurystheus, who would bear the blame and return the hind unharmed
He had spent a year pursuing without harming and would set her free that hour
He swore on the river Styx to build her a temple if she let him pass
He offered her his lion-skin cloak as compensation for the indignity
context: Artemis accepted and let Hercules carry the hind to Eurystheus's court. Eurystheus had hoped Artemis would kill Hercules outright — he claimed the hind for his menagerie. Hercules outsmarted him: he said he would only hand the hind over if Eurystheus came out to take her personally. The moment Eurystheus stepped from the safety of his bronze jar, Hercules let the hind go and she sprinted back to Artemis.

question: Hercules's ninth labor was set by Eurystheus's daughter Admete: bring her the war-belt of Hippolyta, queen of the Amazons. The Amazons were a nation of warrior women who lived along the river Thermodon by the Black Sea. Hippolyta's belt had been given to her by Ares, the god of war. Hercules sailed with a small crew including his friend Theseus. To his surprise, Hippolyta met him in friendship — she had heard of his fame and willingly agreed to give him the belt. Then the queen of the gods intervened with a lie that ended the peace. What did Hera do to start the battle?
answer: Disguised herself as an Amazon and spread the rumor Hercules planned to abduct Hippolyta
choices: Disguised herself as an Amazon and spread the rumor Hercules planned to abduct Hippolyta
Sent a storm cloud over the meeting that made everyone panic
Set fire to Hercules's ship in the harbor as a signal of betrayal
Whispered into Hippolyta's mind that the belt was cursed if given freely
context: The Amazons charged. In the chaos Hercules thought Hippolyta had ordered the attack, killed her, and took the belt by force. Theseus carried off another Amazon, Antiope, as his bride — and the Amazons later invaded Athens to recover her, the only foreign army ever to penetrate the city in Athenian legend.

question: Hercules's sixth labor was to drive off the man-eating Stymphalian birds, a vast flock living in the marshes of Stymphalia in Arcadia. The birds had beaks of bronze, claws of bronze, and feathers they could shoot like arrows. They ate human flesh and their droppings poisoned crops over an enormous area. They were too numerous to shoot down one by one. The marsh was too swampy to drain. Athena gave Hercules a specific gift from the smith god Hephaestus that scared the birds into the air all at once so he could shoot them as they rose. What did Athena give him?
answer: A bronze rattle (krotala) that made an unbearable clattering noise
choices: A bronze rattle (krotala) that made an unbearable clattering noise
A silver hunting horn whose blast deafened all within a mile
A wooden flute that played a tune the birds could not bear
A polished mirror that blinded the birds with sunlight
context: Hercules climbed a nearby mountain, shook the rattle, and the entire flock burst into the sky in panic. He shot down great numbers with his Hydra-poisoned arrows; the survivors fled to the Black Sea, where Jason and the Argonauts later encountered them at the island of Aretias. The labor was completed in a single morning.

question: Before Apollo was born, his pregnant mother Leto was hunted across the earth by a monstrous serpent called the Python, sent by jealous Hera. The Python lived in a cave at the foot of Mount Parnassus, guarding the navel-stone of the world — the stone that Cronus had swallowed in place of the infant Zeus. Apollo, born on the floating island of Delos with his twin sister Artemis, grew fully adult within four days. He then hunted the serpent down. Carrying the bow forged for him by the smith god Hephaestus, he tracked the Python to its cave and killed it with arrows. He buried the great body under what he then made his own most sacred place. What did Apollo found at the cave where he buried the Python?
answer: The oracle of Delphi
choices: The oracle of Delphi
The temple of Artemis at Ephesus
The sanctuary of Olympia
The shrine of Athena at Sounion
context: The Pythia — the priestess who delivered the oracles of Apollo at Delphi — was named for the serpent. She sat on a tripod over a crack in the rock from which sweet-smelling vapors rose. The Pythian Games were held every four years at Delphi to honor Apollo's victory. The phrase 'know thyself' was carved over the temple entrance.

question: The gods agreed that whichever Olympian gave the new city on the Attic peninsula the best gift would become its patron. Two gods competed: Athena, goddess of wisdom, and Poseidon, god of the sea and earthquakes. They met on top of the rock of the Acropolis with King Cecrops as judge and all the citizens watching. Poseidon struck the rock with his trident. A spring of salt water gushed up. He then offered a magnificent war-horse, perfect for battle and for plowing. Athena struck the rock with her spear. A single tree began to grow there — slowly, then full of silver-green leaves. What was Athena's tree?
answer: An olive tree
choices: An olive tree
A laurel tree
A myrtle tree
A cypress tree
context: The citizens chose Athena: the olive gave them oil for cooking and lamps, fruit to eat, wood for ships and houses, and a symbol that became sacred. The city was named Athens. Poseidon, sulking, flooded the plain. Athena's olive tree was burned by Persian invaders in 480 BC but sprouted again the next day from its stump — and an ancient olive still grows on the Acropolis today, said to be a descendant.

question: Demeter, goddess of grain and the harvest, had a beautiful daughter named Persephone, conceived with Zeus. Persephone was picking flowers in a meadow in Sicily with her companions when the earth split open at her feet and Hades, king of the dead, drove his black chariot up out of it. He grabbed her and dragged her down. Demeter wandered the earth searching for her daughter with two flaming torches, neither eating nor drinking nor letting any crops grow. The earth became barren. Zeus finally ordered Hades to return Persephone — but in the underworld Persephone had eaten something there, and the rule was that anyone who ate the food of the dead could never fully return. How many pomegranate seeds did Persephone eat?
answer: Six (or sometimes four, depending on the version)
choices: Six (or sometimes four, depending on the version)
Twelve, one for each month of the calendar year
Three, matching the three Fates who spin the threads
Nine, matching the nine Muses of Mount Helicon
context: Persephone had to spend one month in the underworld with Hades for each seed she ate — six months below, six months above. During the months below, Demeter mourns and nothing grows. The Eleusinian Mysteries, the most sacred religious rite of ancient Greece, retold this story every autumn at Eleusis outside Athens for nearly two thousand years.

question: During her wandering search for her stolen daughter Persephone, the goddess Demeter came in the form of an old woman to the town of Eleusis near Athens. King Celeus and Queen Metaneira gave her hospitality without knowing who she was. Demeter became nurse to their infant son and tried to make him immortal by placing him in the fire each night to burn away his mortal parts — but Metaneira saw and shrieked. Demeter dropped the immortality plan and revealed herself in full divine form. She then taught the older prince of Eleusis a gift to share with all humanity. What did Demeter teach the prince Triptolemus?
answer: How to plant, tend, and harvest grain — that is, the secret of agriculture
choices: How to plant, tend, and harvest grain — that is, the secret of agriculture
How to weave linen cloth from wild flax — gathered from the marshes
How to brew beer and wine from barley — and from the wild grape
How to forge bronze farming tools — without help from any smith
context: Demeter gave Triptolemus a winged chariot drawn by serpents and sent him around the world teaching every nation to plant grain. He became the central hero of the Eleusinian Mysteries — initiates were promised a happier afterlife. Mystery rites at Eleusis ran every September for nearly 2000 years until they were closed by Christian emperors in 392 AD.

question: The Titan Prometheus, whose name means Forethought, took pity on the early humans freezing on the cold earth without fire. He climbed Mount Olympus, lit a torch from the chariot of the sun, hid the flame in a hollow fennel stalk, and carried it down to mankind. When Zeus saw the smoke of cooking fires rising from human settlements at evening, he raged. He had Prometheus chained to a rock in the Caucasus Mountains where every day an eagle came and tore out his liver. Each night the liver grew back so the torture could begin again at dawn. How long did Prometheus suffer on the rock?
answer: Thirty thousand years, until Hercules killed the eagle with an arrow
choices: Thirty thousand years, until Hercules killed the eagle with an arrow
Until the sun god Helios refused to drive his chariot any longer
Until Pandora's jar was finally emptied of all its evils on earth
Until Athena agreed to take his place in chains for one day a year
context: Hercules shot the eagle while passing through the Caucasus on his way to fetch the apples of the Hesperides. Zeus allowed the freeing — Prometheus had also given Zeus a warning that saved him from being overthrown by his own son. Aeschylus wrote the great tragedy Prometheus Bound. The phrase 'fire from heaven' for stolen knowledge comes from this story.

question: When Prometheus stole fire from heaven for mankind, Zeus took his revenge on humanity by ordering the smith god Hephaestus to mold the first woman out of clay. The gods each gave her a gift — Aphrodite gave her beauty, Athena gave her weaving skill, Hermes gave her cunning speech, Apollo gave her music. She was named for the gift-giving: Pandora, all-gifts. Zeus sent her down to earth as a bride for Prometheus's foolish brother Epimetheus — whose name means Afterthought. With her she carried a sealed jar (later mistranslated into Latin as a box) that the gods had told her never to open. She could not resist. What did she find when she lifted the lid?
answer: Every disease, sorrow, and evil flying out into the world, with only Hope left at the bottom
choices: Every disease, sorrow, and evil flying out into the world, with only Hope left at the bottom
A swarm of black serpents that bit her on the hand and crawled out of the room
The thunderbolts of Zeus, which struck her dead the very moment she looked in
A scroll inscribed with every sin Prometheus had committed against the Olympians
context: Hesiod tells the story in Works and Days. Pandora slammed the lid shut just as Hope (Elpis) was about to escape — so Hope alone remained to mankind. The Greek word pithos is a large clay storage jar, not a small box; the 'Pandora's box' translation comes from a 16th-century error by Erasmus.

question: Gaia, the earth goddess, was furious that Zeus and the Olympians had imprisoned her older children the Titans in Tartarus. She gave birth to one last monster to overthrow them: Typhon, a creature so huge his head brushed the stars and his arms reached from sunrise to sunset. His legs were giant snakes and his eyes spat fire. The Olympians fled to Egypt and hid in animal forms — Apollo as a falcon, Hermes as an ibis, Dionysus as a goat. Only Zeus stood his ground. In their first battle, Typhon cut the sinews of Zeus's hands and feet with a sickle, hid them in a bearskin in a cave, and left Zeus helpless. Who stole the sinews back and restored Zeus's strength?
answer: Hermes and Pan, who tricked the dragon guard and slipped the sinews back into Zeus's limbs
choices: Hermes and Pan, who tricked the dragon guard and slipped the sinews back into Zeus's limbs
Athena and Apollo, who killed the dragon guard with arrows
Heracles and Theseus, who stormed the cave in full armor
Aphrodite alone, who seduced the dragon guard to sleep
context: Restored, Zeus pursued Typhon across the sky throwing thunderbolts. He finally pinned the monster under Mount Etna in Sicily, which still smokes and rumbles with Typhon's rage. Mount Etna's volcanic eruptions in classical times were said to be the trapped monster trying to break free.

question: Long after the war with the Titans, Gaia bore one more generation of monsters to attack the Olympians: the Giants. They were enormous warriors with serpent tails for feet, sons of the earth herself. They piled mountain on mountain — Ossa on Pelion — to climb up to Olympus and tear it down. The gods could not kill them alone. An oracle had foretold that the Giants would die only if a particular mortal hero fought alongside the gods. Each Olympian wrestled or shot one giant; the mortal hero delivered each killing blow. Who was the mortal hero whose involvement was necessary?
answer: Hercules
choices: Hercules
Theseus
Achilles
Perseus
context: The Gigantomachy (battle of the giants) was a favorite subject of Greek temple decoration. The great altar of Pergamon (now in Berlin) shows the entire battle in massive relief sculpture. Athena killed Pallas. Apollo and Hercules killed Ephialtes. Dionysus killed Eurytus with his thyrsus. The leader Alcyoneus could not die in his birthplace, so Hercules dragged him over the border and killed him there.

question: The Olympic Games were held every four years at Olympia in the western Peloponnese for nearly 1200 years — from 776 BC until the Christian Emperor Theodosius banned them in 393 AD. Greek legend gave them three founders. Some said Hercules founded the games after completing one of his labors and marking off the sacred precinct of Zeus with paces of his own foot. Others said the games began after a chariot race between a mortal prince and his future father-in-law, with the king crashing and dying when the prince's accomplice (the future father-in-law's charioteer Myrtilus) sabotaged the wheels. Who was the prince in that founding chariot race?
answer: Pelops, after whom the Peloponnese is named
choices: Pelops, after whom the Peloponnese is named
Cadmus, the founder of Thebes
Theseus, before he became king of Athens
Bellerophon, before he tamed Pegasus
context: Pelops was racing King Oenomaus of Pisa for the hand of his daughter Hippodamia. Oenomaus had killed thirteen previous suitors. Pelops won by bribing the king's charioteer to replace the bronze axle-pins with beeswax. The Peloponnese (Pelops's island) is named for him. The Olympic stadium and the Temple of Zeus housed Phidias's huge gold-and-ivory statue, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

question: The master craftsman Daedalus had designed King Minos's labyrinth on Crete to hold the Minotaur. After he helped Princess Ariadne save Theseus by giving her the ball of thread, Minos imprisoned Daedalus and his young son Icarus in a high tower. Daedalus, an inventor, gathered feathers shed by birds and built two pairs of wings with the feathers fixed to a wooden frame by beeswax. He warned Icarus before they leaped from the tower: do not fly too low, for the sea spray would soak the feathers; and do not fly too high, for one specific reason. What was the danger of flying too high?
answer: The sun would melt the wax holding the feathers together
choices: The sun would melt the wax holding the feathers together
The thin air of the upper sky would burst his lungs in panic
The eagles of Olympus would attack him as a rival to the gods
The clouds were the floor of Olympus, and Zeus would strike him down
context: Icarus, dazzled by flight, climbed higher and higher. The wax softened, then dripped, then ran. The feathers fell away. Icarus plummeted into the sea now called the Icarian Sea between Samos and Mykonos. Daedalus flew on alone to Sicily, where he hid himself at the court of King Cocalus. Bruegel painted Icarus's tiny splash in the corner of a busy harbor — almost no one notices the boy falling.

question: King Acrisius of Argos consulted the oracle at Delphi and was told that his daughter Danae would bear a son who would one day kill him. To prevent the prophecy, Acrisius locked his daughter in an underground bronze chamber with only a small opening to the sky. Zeus, captivated by Danae's beauty, found a way through the opening anyway — he came to her in an unusual form, not as the bull he used for Europa or the swan he used for Leda. What form did Zeus take to enter Danae's bronze chamber?
answer: A shower of golden rain
choices: A shower of golden rain
A breath of summer wind
An eagle clutching pomegranates in its talons
A column of silver smoke from below
context: Danae bore Perseus from this union. Acrisius, terrified of the prophecy, sealed mother and infant son into a wooden chest and threw them into the sea. They washed ashore on the island of Seriphos. Years later, exactly as the oracle had said, Perseus killed Acrisius — by accident, with a discus thrown wide at a funeral games.

question: King Polydectes of Seriphos wanted to marry Danae but was blocked by her grown son Perseus. So he tricked Perseus into promising any wedding gift the king named — and then demanded the impossible: the head of Medusa, one of three Gorgon sisters with snakes for hair, whose direct gaze turned any living thing instantly to stone. Hermes gave Perseus an adamant sickle to behead her. Athena gave him a polished bronze shield so he could see Medusa's reflection without looking at her directly. The Hesperides nymphs also gave him a cap of darkness from Hades and a wallet to hold the head. What did the winged sandals Hermes lent him let Perseus do?
answer: Fly through the air all the way to the Gorgons' western cave
choices: Fly through the air all the way to the Gorgons' western cave
Walk on water across the Aegean Sea without sinking down
Run faster than any horse over the mountains of all Greece
Step between living and ghost worlds at any moment he chose
context: Perseus first had to find the Graeae — three gray sisters who shared one eye and one tooth between them — and steal the eye to force them to tell him where the nymphs lived. He flew to the Gorgons' cave at the edge of the world, beheaded Medusa using her reflection in his shield, and from her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus.

question: Flying home from killing Medusa with her head in his magical wallet, Perseus passed over the kingdom of Ethiopia. He saw a beautiful young woman chained to a rock by the sea, with people weeping on the shore behind her. Her mother Queen Cassiopeia had boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, the Nereids. Poseidon had punished the kingdom by sending a sea monster called Cetus to ravage the coast. The oracle had said the only way to stop the monster was to sacrifice the princess Andromeda. Perseus negotiated quickly with her parents King Cepheus and Queen Cassiopeia — if he killed the monster, he would marry her. What did Perseus use to defeat Cetus?
answer: He pulled Medusa's head from his wallet and turned the sea monster to stone
choices: He pulled Medusa's head from his wallet and turned the sea monster to stone
He drove his sword between the monster's third and fourth scale-row
He dropped boulders from the air onto the monster's head until it sank
He used Hermes's caduceus to charm the monster to sleep underwater
context: After the marriage, Andromeda's previous fiance Phineus arrived with a hundred armed men to claim her. Perseus uncovered Medusa's head again and turned them all to stone in a single moment. Andromeda was later set in the night sky as a constellation, along with her mother Cassiopeia (still seated upside down on her throne as punishment for the original boast), her father Cepheus, the sea monster Cetus, and Perseus himself with his sword arm raised.

question: On his way home from killing Medusa, Perseus passed over the western edge of the world where the Titan Atlas stood holding up the sky on his shoulders. Atlas had a beautiful garden full of golden fruit and was afraid of a prophecy that a son of Zeus would one day come and steal them. Atlas refused Perseus hospitality and tried to drive him away. Perseus, exhausted from his flight, did not have the patience to fight him. He pulled out the head of Medusa and turned Atlas's stare to stone. What did Atlas become?
answer: The Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa, holding the sky on their peaks
choices: The Atlas Mountains in northwest Africa, holding the sky on their peaks
A pillar of granite at the gates of the western world
A lone cypress tree on the African shore, taller than any other
A statue of marble at the entrance to the Gardens of the Hesperides
context: Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses. The Atlas Mountains span Morocco, Algeria, and Tunisia today; the Atlantic Ocean (Sea of Atlas) and our word atlas for a book of maps both come from the same name. The ancient prophecy was finally fulfilled when Hercules — also a son of Zeus — came to the same garden for the apples.

question: Jason of Iolcus was ordered by his usurping uncle Pelias to fetch the Golden Fleece from Colchis at the far end of the Black Sea — a quest meant to kill him. Jason had the master shipwright Argus build the largest ship ever built, with a magical timber from the speaking oak of Zeus's grove at Dodona set into the prow. He assembled a crew of the greatest heroes of Greece including Hercules, Orpheus, Castor and Pollux. They came at last to the entrance of the Black Sea: a pair of cliffs called the Symplegades or Clashing Rocks that smashed together whenever a ship tried to pass between them. How did the Argonauts get through?
answer: They sent a dove between the rocks first; it lost only tail feathers, and they rowed through the gap before the cliffs reset
choices: They sent a dove between the rocks first; it lost only tail feathers, and they rowed through the gap before the cliffs reset
Orpheus played such beautiful music on his lyre that the great rocks froze entirely in place for an entire day
Hercules pushed both cliffs apart with his bare hands and held them open while the Argo rowed past in safety
They waited for a moonless night when the rocks could not see and slipped past in total darkness without sound
context: The Argo's stern was clipped slightly by the closing rocks but the ship survived. From that day forward the Clashing Rocks were fixed in place — the prophecy said they would freeze if any ship ever passed between them safely. The Symplegades were near the mouth of the Bosphorus, where the Black Sea meets the Mediterranean today.

question: The Argonauts landed at the kingdom of the blind seer Phineus on the coast of Thrace. Phineus had once been a great prophet to whom Apollo had given the gift of sight — but he had abused the gift, revealing too many of Zeus's secrets to mortals. Zeus blinded him and set on him a curse: every time a meal was set in front of Phineus, three winged monsters with women's faces and birds' bodies would swoop down from the sky, snatch most of the food away, and foul whatever they left behind so it could not be eaten. Phineus was starving. He promised the Argonauts the prophecies they needed if they could drive off the monsters. Which two Argonauts were able to chase them away?
answer: Calais and Zetes, the winged sons of the North Wind Boreas
choices: Calais and Zetes, the winged sons of the North Wind Boreas
Castor and Polydeuces, the twin sons of Zeus and Leda
Idas and Lynceus, the keen-eyed brothers of Messenia
Telamon and Peleus, the brothers from Aegina
context: Calais and Zetes had wings of their own and could fly. They drove the Harpies south across the sea until they reached the Strophades Islands, where the Harpies finally swore on the river Styx never to torment Phineus again. The grateful seer then warned the Argonauts about the Clashing Rocks and the dove trick.

question: When the Argonauts reached Colchis at the eastern edge of the Black Sea, King Aeetes refused to hand over the Golden Fleece unless Jason performed three impossible tasks. First, he had to yoke two fire-breathing bronze-hooved bulls and plow a field with them. Second, he had to sow that field with the teeth of a dragon — armed warriors would spring from each tooth and attack him. Third, he had to defeat the warriors. Aeetes's daughter Medea, struck by Aphrodite's arrows with love for Jason, secretly came to him at night with a magical ointment to coat his skin and his armor for one day, making him invulnerable to fire and weapons. She also told him one specific trick to defeat the army of warriors. What was the trick?
answer: Throw a single heavy stone into the middle of them, and they would fight each other to the death
choices: Throw a single heavy stone into the middle of them, and they would fight each other to the death
Sing the lullaby of the river Phasis softly over the field to put them all back to sleep at once
Pour the remaining ointment on the ground around them to dissolve them where they stood armed
Call out King Aeetes's full name three times to confuse their orders and scatter them in panic
context: Jason did exactly that. The earth-born warriors fell on each other in confusion and killed each other to the last man. Medea then drugged the never-sleeping dragon that guarded the Fleece and Jason snatched it from the oak tree. They fled together — Medea would later kill her own brother to slow Aeetes's pursuit, scattering his pieces in the sea so the king had to stop to gather them for burial.

question: Theseus was born in the city of Troezen across the Saronic Gulf from Athens. His mother Aethra told him as a young man that his real father was King Aegeus of Athens, who had left a sword and a pair of sandals hidden under a great rock with instructions that the boy could come find his father once he was strong enough to roll the rock aside. Theseus lifted the rock at sixteen, took the sword and sandals, and chose the dangerous overland route to Athens instead of the safe sea journey. The road to Athens was infested with bandits and monsters. One bandit named Procrustes had a particular habit involving an iron bed by the roadside. What did Procrustes do to his guests?
answer: Stretched short guests until they fit the bed and lopped off the limbs of tall guests to make them fit
choices: Stretched short guests until they fit the bed and lopped off the limbs of tall guests to make them fit
Robbed each one and left them all to starve tied tightly to the iron bed for the next several days
Cooked them alive on a brazen bed-frame placed over a deep pit of hot coals dug into the floor
Sold them as slaves to merchant ships docking each evening at the nearby harbor town of Eleusis
context: Theseus served Procrustes the same treatment he had served his guests — adjusting him to fit his own bed by amputation. The phrase 'Procrustean bed' for forcing things into the wrong shape comes from this story. Theseus killed five other major bandits on the road: Periphetes the club-bearer, Sinis the pine-bender, the Crommyonian Sow, Sciron the cliff-kicker, and Cercyon the wrestler.

question: After Theseus had been king of Athens for many years, he made a pact with his closest friend Pirithous, king of the Lapiths in Thessaly. The two heroes had grown bored and decided each would marry a daughter of Zeus. Theseus chose to abduct the twelve-year-old Helen of Sparta (who was later rescued by her brothers Castor and Polydeuces and grew up to start the Trojan War). For Pirithous, they aimed higher: Persephone, the wife of Hades himself. They walked down to the underworld and Hades received them with apparent hospitality, inviting them to sit on a stone bench while he considered their proposal. What happened when they sat down?
answer: Their flesh fused to the stone and they could not stand back up
choices: Their flesh fused to the stone and they could not stand back up
The earth swallowed the bench down into Tartarus pit
Hades changed them both into bats that hung from the cave ceiling
Cerberus chained them by the necks to the gates of the underworld
context: Hercules later came to the underworld as his twelfth labor and saw the two friends rooted to the bench. He pulled Theseus free, leaving most of Theseus's thighs stuck to the stone — Athenians were said ever after to have thin thighs because of this. Pirithous, the actual instigator, was left in the underworld forever; the rock would not yield him.

question: Bellerophon was a young prince of Corinth, falsely accused of trying to seduce the queen of Tiryns. The king of Tiryns sent him to King Iobates of Lycia carrying a sealed letter that instructed Iobates to kill the bearer. Iobates was a guest-host and could not break the sacred laws of hospitality by killing Bellerophon directly — so he sent him to fight the monster Chimera, a fire-breathing creature with a lion's head, a goat's middle, and a serpent's tail. Bellerophon needed a flying mount. He slept in the temple of Athena and the goddess appeared in a dream with a golden bridle. The bridle would let Bellerophon tame the winged horse Pegasus, who had sprung from the severed neck of Medusa. Where did Bellerophon find Pegasus to bridle him?
answer: Drinking at the spring Pirene on the citadel of Corinth
choices: Drinking at the spring Pirene on the citadel of Corinth
Grazing in the meadows of the Hesperides at world's end
Sleeping in the stables of King Aeetes of Colchis
Resting in the cave of the centaur Chiron on Mount Pelion
context: Bellerophon flew over the Chimera and killed it from the air by jamming a lump of lead onto the tip of his spear — the lump melted in the monster's fiery breath and poured down its throat. Later Bellerophon tried to ride Pegasus all the way to Olympus to join the gods. Zeus sent a gadfly to bite Pegasus, who threw Bellerophon off in mid-air. Bellerophon survived the fall but spent the rest of his life crippled and despised, alone in a marsh.

question: Oedipus was a young man traveling toward Thebes on foot. The city was being terrorized by a monster called the Sphinx — a creature with the head of a woman, the body of a lion, and the wings of an eagle. She sat on a cliff above the road and asked every traveler the same riddle. Anyone who answered wrong was thrown off the cliff and devoured. The reward for the right answer was the throne of Thebes — Queen Jocasta had recently been widowed when her husband King Laius was murdered on the road. The riddle was: What walks on four legs in the morning, two legs at noon, and three legs in the evening? What did Oedipus answer?
answer: Man — crawling as an infant, walking upright as an adult, leaning on a staff in old age
choices: Man — crawling as an infant, walking upright as an adult, leaning on a staff in old age
Time itself — counted in dawns, noons, and twilights of each day
A river — narrow at the source, wide in the plain, branching at the delta
A tree — sapling spreading roots, trunk standing tall, branches drooping
context: When Oedipus gave the answer, the Sphinx threw herself off the cliff in fury. He entered Thebes as a hero, was given the throne, and married the widowed queen Jocasta. He did not know that the murdered King Laius — whom he had killed in a quarrel at a crossroads on his journey — was his real father, and Jocasta was his real mother. The full horror of what he had done would not be revealed for many years.

question: Years after Oedipus had become king of Thebes and fathered four children by Queen Jocasta, a plague struck the city. The oracle at Delphi declared the plague would only end when the killer of the old King Laius was found and exiled. Oedipus, not knowing he himself was the killer, swore terrible curses on the murderer and ordered the investigation. The blind prophet Tiresias warned him to stop digging. A shepherd was found who had received Laius's infant son to be exposed on a mountainside long ago — the shepherd had taken pity on the baby and given it to a Corinthian shepherd instead. The Corinthian had given the baby to King Polybus of Corinth, who raised the infant as his own son. Oedipus finally understood: he himself was that baby. What did Jocasta do when she realized she had married her own son?
answer: Hanged herself in their bedchamber
choices: Hanged herself in their bedchamber
Drank a cup of poison
Drowned in the river Ismenus
Leapt from the high citadel
context: Oedipus found Jocasta hanging, took the long gold pins from her dress, and stabbed himself in both eyes with them — over and over until blood ran down his cheeks. He cried out that he could no longer bear to look upon what he had done. His daughter Antigone led him into exile to wander as a blind beggar. Sophocles wrote two great plays about him: Oedipus Rex and Oedipus at Colonus.

question: After Oedipus went into exile, his two sons Eteocles and Polyneices were supposed to share the throne of Thebes by alternating years. Eteocles refused to step down at the end of his year. Polyneices raised an army to take the throne by force — the Seven Against Thebes. In the battle, the two brothers met in single combat and killed each other simultaneously. Their uncle Creon, now king, decreed that Eteocles (the defender) would be buried with honors but Polyneices (the attacker) would be left on the plain for dogs and vultures, with the death penalty for anyone who tried to bury him. Their sister Antigone defied the decree. What did she use to bury her brother's body?
answer: Dust scattered three times over the corpse, which counted as a symbolic burial under Greek law
choices: Dust scattered three times over the corpse, which counted as a symbolic burial under Greek law
A grave dug at midnight by her own hands with a wooden spade borrowed from the city potter
A pyre of cedar logs lit secretly in the foothills outside the city walls beneath the stars
A sealed urn of polished bronze hidden away in the royal family tomb in the heart of Thebes
context: Creon sentenced Antigone to be sealed alive in a stone tomb. His son Haemon, who was engaged to her, killed himself when he found her hanging in the tomb. Creon's wife Eurydice killed herself when she heard her son was dead. Sophocles wrote the play Antigone, which has become the foundational Western text about the conflict between conscience and the law of the state.

question: The house of Atreus was cursed for generations after one specific terrible meal. The brothers Atreus and Thyestes were rival claimants to the throne of Mycenae. Thyestes had seduced Atreus's wife Aerope and stolen a sacred golden lamb from his flock as proof of kingship. Atreus pretended to reconcile and invited Thyestes to a great banquet. He served a magnificent stew. After Thyestes had eaten his fill, Atreus brought out a silver platter showing him what the stew had been made of. What did the platter contain?
answer: The heads, hands, and feet of Thyestes's own three sons, whom Atreus had murdered and cooked
choices: The heads, hands, and feet of Thyestes's own three sons, whom Atreus had murdered and cooked
The body of Thyestes's wife stitched back together after dismemberment
The bones of their father Pelops, dug up from his grave at Olympia
The pelt of the golden lamb stuffed with Thyestes's own murdered slaves
context: Thyestes vomited up the meal and cursed the entire house of Atreus. The curse fell on Atreus's son Agamemnon (killed in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra), on his grandson Orestes (driven mad by the Furies for avenging his father), and continued for generations. Aeschylus wrote the entire Oresteia trilogy about how the curse was finally broken at Athens by the founding of the law courts.

question: King Agamemnon, commander of the Greeks at Troy, sailed home to Mycenae after ten years of war bringing the captive princess Cassandra with him as concubine. His wife Clytemnestra had been waiting all those years with one specific grievance — Agamemnon had sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia to Artemis at Aulis to get a favorable wind for the Greek fleet to sail. While Agamemnon was at Troy, Clytemnestra had taken Agamemnon's cousin Aegisthus as her lover (Aegisthus's father Thyestes had been the victim of the cannibal feast — so this whole drama was the curse playing out again). Clytemnestra welcomed Agamemnon home, drew him a hot bath, and walked him toward it on a long purple carpet. What did she do once he was in the bath?
answer: Threw a net over him so he could not move and axed him to death
choices: Threw a net over him so he could not move and axed him to death
Locked the bathroom door and waited for him to drown in his sleep
Stabbed him through the throat with the same sword he had used at Troy
Poured boiling oil into the tub from a vessel hidden behind the curtain
context: Clytemnestra also killed Cassandra in the same hour, axing her in the courtyard. Cassandra had foreseen all of it and walked to her death predicting it aloud — and as always, no one believed her. The story is told in Aeschylus's Agamemnon, the first play of the Oresteia trilogy.

question: Orestes, the young son of Agamemnon and Clytemnestra, was sent away from Mycenae as a boy and grew up at the court of King Strophius of Phocis. There he became sworn brother to Strophius's son Pylades. The oracle at Delphi commanded Orestes to return to Mycenae and avenge his murdered father by killing the murderers — his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. Orestes did exactly that. The instant his mother was dead, three monstrous female spirits with snakes in their hair appeared and began chasing him across Greece, screaming for his blood. Who were the spirits who hunted Orestes?
answer: The Furies, who hunted any child who killed a parent
choices: The Furies, who hunted any child who killed a parent
The Sirens, drawn to the smell of family blood
The Harpies, sent by Apollo as a test of nerve
The Graeae, the gray sisters with one shared eye
context: Orestes finally took refuge at Athens. Athena herself set up the first court of law to try him — twelve human jurors, with Athena as judge. They split 6-6, and Athena cast the deciding vote for acquittal, arguing that the father's claim outweighed the mother's. The Furies were transformed into the Eumenides, the Kindly Ones, with a sacred grove at Athens. Aeschylus's trilogy ended with this founding of the rule of law over the rule of blood.

question: After the Trojan Horse let the Greeks into Troy at night, the city was sacked with unspeakable brutality. Old King Priam was butchered at his own altar by Achilles's son Neoptolemus. Cassandra was dragged from the temple of Athena where she had taken sanctuary. The young widow Andromache, wife of the dead Hector, was made the concubine of Neoptolemus. She begged for the life of her infant son. The Greeks debated. Odysseus argued that the boy must die so he could not grow up to take revenge for the war. The decision was made. What did the Greeks do to Andromache's small son Astyanax?
answer: Threw him from the highest tower of Troy
choices: Threw him from the highest tower of Troy
Drowned him in the river Scamander outside the walls
Buried him alive with Priam in the royal tomb
Carried him to Greece as a hostage but he died on the voyage
context: Euripides wrote The Trojan Women about this scene. Andromache's lament for her child — knowing as a Trojan princess that she could not even ransom him — is one of the most devastating speeches in surviving Greek drama. The Greeks paid for the cruelty: most of their leaders died on the voyage home, or arrived to find treason waiting.

question: Queen Niobe of Thebes had fourteen beautiful children — seven sons and seven daughters. She boasted publicly that she was a greater mother than the goddess Leto, who had only borne two: Apollo and Artemis. Leto's twins took the insult personally. They came down from Olympus armed with their bows. Apollo went after Niobe's sons, hunting them down one by one. Artemis took the daughters. The youngest daughter clung to her mother's knee begging for mercy. What happened to Niobe after all fourteen of her children were dead at her feet?
answer: She turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping
choices: She turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping
She was made queen of the underworld by Hades in her grief
She wandered the earth as a hag for a thousand years until Zeus pitied her
She killed herself by leaping from the citadel of Thebes that same night
context: Ovid describes the slow petrification in the Metamorphoses — Niobe's body gradually hardened to marble even as her tears went on flowing. The 'Weeping Rock' on Mount Sipylus in modern Turkey has a face-like outline and a spring that runs down it; locals showed it to ancient travelers as the actual Niobe. The phrase 'Niobe in tears' for grief beyond words comes from this story.

question: Tantalus was a son of Zeus and a wealthy king of Sipylus in Lydia. He was invited to dine with the gods on Olympus — a unique honor for a mortal. He repaid the hospitality by stealing nectar and ambrosia to share with his mortal friends, and by an even worse offense. To test whether the gods could really tell omniscience apart from cleverness, he killed his own son Pelops, cooked the body, and served it to the Olympians at a feast. Demeter, distracted by grief for her missing daughter Persephone, ate part of Pelops's shoulder before the gods realized. Zeus reassembled Pelops with an ivory shoulder replacement and condemned Tantalus to a specific eternal punishment in Tartarus. What was the punishment?
answer: Standing in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, both forever pulling away when he reached
choices: Standing in a pool of water beneath a fruit tree, both forever pulling away when he reached
Rolling a great stone forever uphill that always rolled back to the bottom at the summit
Lashed to a fiery wheel that spun across the sky forever through the dark underworld halls
Eating his own growing liver while it grew back nightly beneath the beak of a huge eagle
context: The English word 'tantalize' comes from Tantalus. His descendants carried the curse: his son Pelops (the one with the ivory shoulder) raced for Hippodamia at Olympia; his grandsons Atreus and Thyestes feasted on each other's children; his great-grandson Agamemnon was axed in the bath; his great-great-grandson Orestes was hunted by the Furies.

question: Sisyphus was the founding king of Corinth, famous in Greek myth as the cleverest of mortal men. He cheated the gods repeatedly. When Zeus came to take his daughter the river-nymph Aegina, Sisyphus told her father the river god Asopus where she was, ruining Zeus's plans. As punishment Zeus sent Thanatos (Death) to take Sisyphus to the underworld. Sisyphus tricked Thanatos into trying on a pair of handcuffs and locked Death into his own chains — for a time no human anywhere on earth could die, until Ares freed Thanatos. Sisyphus then talked his way back out of the underworld a second time by claiming his wife had not buried him properly. The gods finally caught him. What was his eternal punishment?
answer: Roll a huge boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down every time he reached the top
choices: Roll a huge boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down every time he reached the top
Stand chest-deep in the river Lethe, with the dark water evaporating each time he stooped to drink
Plow a field of grey stones with two ghost-oxen that vanished into thin air each evening at sunset
Build a wall of polished brass around the gates of Tartarus that crumbled away to dust overnight
context: The image of Sisyphus pushing his stone became one of the most-quoted symbols of human existence in Western thought. Albert Camus wrote The Myth of Sisyphus in 1942 arguing that we must imagine Sisyphus happy — finding meaning in the struggle itself, not in any final achievement. The Sisyphean task became a phrase for any work without lasting result.
